title: The page that explains pricing without a number
metaTitle: Explain price without a public number
excerpt: If you cannot publish a price, publish what changes it, what is included, and how a buyer starts. A page that only says contact us for pricing is a closed door.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper, the shape of a price written out when the number itself stays off the page.
caption: A pen on lined paper. Publish the shape of the price when you cannot publish the number. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a pricing page include when you cannot show a number?
faqs.answer: Say why a single number would be false, list the few things that move the price, and list what is included and what is not. Then give one way to start. Contact us, with nothing around it, does not help a buyer decide whether a conversation is worth the hour.

faqs.question: Should you invent a from price to fill the page?
faqs.answer: No. A figure you will not honor is a trick, not a shape. Bands named by the situation, with no currency symbol, are more honest than a strikethrough. If you are only nervous, consider publishing the real number instead of hiding it.

faqs.question: How should sales talk about a price the site does not print?
faqs.answer: Use the same drivers, inclusions, and exclusions the page lists. An exception should be named as an exception. A private calculator, if you have one, should take the same inputs the public page already taught the buyer.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
If you cannot publish a price, publish the shape of the price. What changes it. What is included. What is not. How a buyer starts. A pricing page without public prices can still be a page a serious person finishes. "Contact us for pricing," with nothing around it, is a closed door.

The shape is not a tease. It is the information a buyer uses to decide whether a conversation is worth the hour. Give them that, and then give them a way to talk.

## Say why the number is absent

Tell the truth in one sentence. The price depends on how many sites, how many seats, how complex the catalog, or which of a few packages the work falls into. A custom engagement depends on the pages and the states. A product depends on the plan and the usage that actually moves the cost.

Skip the theater. "We tailor every partnership to your unique journey" does not explain a missing number. A buyer has heard it before. They are trying to learn whether you are in the range they can even discuss. You can say the range is wide, and still say what makes it wide.

If a regulation, a procurement rule, or a genuine custom scope is the reason, say that. If the reason is habit, consider publishing a number. This piece is for the case where a single number would be false. It is not a trick for hiding a number you are simply nervous about. Nervousness is a bad information architecture.

Hanabi's own engagements vary with the work, so a public rate card would pretend a precision the work does not have. The honest substitute, for us or for you, is the shape: pages, states, what is out, and whether the work is a fixed release or an ongoing relationship. The first conversation can put a number on a known list. It cannot put a number on a vibe. Your page should say that, in your words.

## What changes the price

List the real drivers, in the buyer's language. Seats, locations, languages, transaction volume, the number of templates, the number of integrations that already exist, the deadline. Three to six drivers is a useful list. A list of twenty is a questionnaire you were afraid to call a form.

Say which driver moves the price a lot, if you can say it without a spreadsheet. "A second language is a phase, not a line item we hide." "Each additional template is smaller than the first, because the system exists." You are teaching the buyer how to think. That is the page's job.

Say what does not change the price, if people always ask. "We do not charge per stakeholder in the review." "View-only users are included." Negative space in the price is part of the shape. It prevents a sales call from opening on a fear.

If you have two or three bands, name them by the situation, not by precious metal. "A first marketing site." "A site plus the product UI." "An ongoing partnership." Under each, list what is in and what is out. You can do this with no currency symbol at all. The bands are still more honest than a single contact button.

Do not invent precision. Ranges you do not mean, "from" prices that nobody pays, and strikethrough anchors are how a shape becomes a trick. If you are not willing to honor a figure, it does not go on the page.

## What is included, and what starts the work

Included is a list of objects. Workshops, the pages, the build, QA on a phone, the basic content model, the handover of the repo and the accounts. Use your real list. A buyer should be able to tell a colleague what they would get.

Not included is the same kind of list. A new name. Illustration for every section. Ongoing marketing. Copywriting if you expect the client to bring the sentences. Say so. The out list is not a lack of generosity. It is how both sides avoid a fight in month two.

Say what you need from them before a number can be real. Access to the current site, a decider, the offer in a sentence, examples of proof they are willing to show. If those are missing, any number is a guess. The page can say that without scolding. "A quote follows a list of pages and states" is a process. It is also a kindness.

Then say how to start. One action. A call, a form with three useful questions, or an email if that is truly how you work. The questions on the form should be the drivers, not "tell us about yourself" and a blank box the size of a novel. Ask for the audience, the offer, and what they think the pages are. You can ask for timing. You do not need their stack, their revenue, and their childhood.

Reply expectations belong here, in a sentence you will keep. "We answer within two working days" only if you do. A false promise on the pricing page is a strange place to start a relationship about money.

## How the page should read in the first screen

The first screen carries the reason, the drivers, and the action. Nielsen Norman Group's research is the reason to be this blunt. People often leave in 10 to 20 seconds. A value they can use has to show up in about 10. "Contact us for pricing" fails that test. "Price follows the number of templates, languages, and whether we are building the product UI" can pass it, if it is true.

Use a heading that states the situation. "How pricing works" is acceptable. "Invest in your future" is not a pricing heading. Google's title-link guidance wants a descriptive title and one clear main heading. Make the title agree with the heading. A buyer searching for whether you publish prices should land on a page that admits the question.

Keep the visual system of the rest of the site. A pricing page that suddenly looks like a startup template, with three columns and a highlighted middle, will invent a middle tier you do not sell. If you do not have three packages, do not draw three packages. A single column with drivers and an out list is a more confident design than a fake good-better-best.

Type should be ordinary and readable. This is a page people will read more carefully than the homepage, if you give them something to read. Do not set the drivers in a display face at low contrast. The WCAG principle of perceivable content is not a slogan. It is whether a finance partner can read the out list on a train.

Link to one example of the work, so the shape connects to an object. One project with a constraint does more than a strip of logos. Down the Cove, an ecommerce migration and redesign, and Thomas Bewick, an editorial heritage site, are different shapes of work. Leadly, a product interface, is another. Pick the cousin of the job the buyer is pricing. Showing every project and hoping is how the page becomes a portfolio with a contact form taped on.

## What sales must not contradict

The page becomes false the moment a salesperson offers a different shape in the first email. If the page says languages are a later phase, the email should not fold a second language into the first number to win the week. Align the talk track with the drivers. When a deal needs an exception, name it as an exception.

Give sales the same list the page has. Drivers, included, excluded, what you need before a quote. A private calculator can exist. If it exists, the inputs should be the drivers on the page, not a second set of mysteries. Otherwise the buyer will feel the page was a brochure and the real price lives in a back room. Some of that is inevitable. The size of the gap is a choice.

Update the page when the drivers change. A new packaging decision that never reaches the site will be "corrected" on calls until nobody remembers the correction. Date the notes in your internal doc. The public page can stay free of a changelog tone. It still has to match this quarter.

Do not add a number in a case study that you will not put on the pricing page. A project write-up that says "a six-week engagement" or a fee is a public price, whether you meant it or not. Hanabi does not invent timelines or fees in public write-ups for this reason. Your proof can describe the constraint and the decision without becoming a rate card by accident.

## A buyer should leave knowing the next step

Read the page as the finance partner who was forwarded a link and has eight minutes. They should be able to say what moves the price, what they would receive, what they must bring, and how to ask for a number. If they can only say "we have to get on a call," the page did not do its job. Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether someone leaves having learned enough to achieve a goal. On this page the goal is a qualified conversation, not a surprise.

The conversation itself can then be specific. Pages, states, outs, and which driver dominates. That is a better hour than discovering the shape from scratch while everyone pretends the number is the only topic.

Security and procurement often arrive in the same week as price. A buyer who understands the shape will ask where the data lives next. The piece on [a security page a buyer can finish](/blog/a-security-page-that-a-buyer-can-finish) is the next read, so the trust question is answered with the same plainness as the money question.

When you want the shape of a studio engagement, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The offers there have boundaries. A pricing page without a number should have boundaries too.
